extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, patent attorneys, law firms representing clients before the USPTO (and counsel handling USPTO disciplinary/compliance matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and disciplinary criteria under the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct relating to communication with organizational clients, informed consent, disclosure, independent professional judgment, and related sanctions; illustrated by a Final Order in a disciplinary settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.102(a) — Abide by client's decisions and consult on means
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation and shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consulting with an entity client through a non-fiduciary agent instead of directly consulting with the entity's decisionmaker (here, the sole owner) violates this provision. The Final Order uses Respondent's consultation through Mavexar (a non-fiduciary intermediary) rather than direct consultation with Mellaconic's owner as the predicate for violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(1) — Promptly inform client when informed consent is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which the client's informed consent is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informing an entity client via a non-fiduciary agent rather than directly (e.g., failing to tell the client's owner about the firm's longstanding referral relationship with IP Edge/Mavexar) constitutes a violation. The order emphasizes that the firm did not inform Mellaconic's owner that Sand, Sebolt & Wernow received hundreds of referrals from IP Edge/Mavexar.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — Reasonably consult with client about means to accomplish objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing litigation on behalf of an entity client without direct consultation with the entity's decisionmaker (instead communicating through a non-fiduciary intermediary) can violate this duty. The Order finds Respondent failed to consult Mellaconic's owner about filing litigation prior to doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — Keep the client reasonably informed about status
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informing an entity client of status through a non-fiduciary agent (rather than directly informing the client's owner) is a violation when it results in the owner not being reasonably informed that litigation was filed or about developments. The Final Order cites failure to directly communicate with the owner regarding litigation status.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — Explain matters to permit informed decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of noncompliance include failing to explain the risks of patent litigation, failing to explain the implications of the client's consulting agreement with a non-fiduciary intermediary (Mavexar), and failing to disclose that the client stood to receive only a small percentage of proceeds while bearing 100% of litigation costs. The Order cites these informational failures as violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.201 — Independent professional judgment and candid advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on communications through a non-fiduciary intermediary rather than directly with the client can undermine independent judgment and candid advice. The Order finds that communicating through Mavexar rather than directly with Mellaconic's owner violated § 11.201.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose referral relationships and relevant relationships with intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner should disclose material relationships and referral histories (e.g., longstanding referral relationship with an intermediary) that could affect informed consent or client decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order emphasizes that failing to inform the client that the firm had a longstanding relationship with IP Edge/Mavexar and received hundreds of referrals from them contributed to violations of disclosure/informed-consent rules. Disclosure of such relationships is necessary to permit informed client decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct communication with organizational clients (especially sole-owner entities)
rubrics_metrics.description: When representing an organizational client that is solely owned, a practitioner must directly communicate with and consult the owner's decisionmaker rather than relying exclusively on third-party intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order treats the practice of communicating only through Mavexar (for over a year and until after litigation filings) as the central misconduct. Engagement, litigation decisions, and status communications must be directly made to the entity's decisionmaker when appropriate to satisfy consultation and informed-consent requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement agreements and delivery/explanation to client
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement agreements should be provided to and discussed directly with the client or client decisionmaker, and their terms (including who may communicate with counsel) should be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this matter, the firm's engagement agreement was routed through the intermediary and not directly sent to or explained to the sole owner. The Order highlights that practitioners should ensure the client themselves receive and understand engagement terms, not rely solely on intermediaries to handle that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and explanation of financial arrangements affecting client decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must explain financial consequences of representation and related agreements (e.g., division of proceeds, who bears litigation costs) to permit informed client decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order notes Respondent failed to explain that Mellaconic would receive only 5% of net proceeds while bearing 100% of litigation costs, and that costs were advanced by the intermediary on a recourse basis. Such material financial information must be explained directly to the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of intermediary's fiduciary status and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner should disclose and explain whether an intermediary (consultant/manager) is a fiduciary and the legal implications of the intermediary's status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consulting agreement expressly stated Mavexar was not a fiduciary; Respondent did not explain the potential consequences of that fact to the client. Practitioners must explain how an intermediary's non-fiduciary status could affect decisionmaking and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors in discipline: acknowledgement, contrition, cooperation, remedial measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging actions, demonstrating contrition, cooperating with investigation, and implementing remedial procedures can be mitigation considerations in disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order cites Respondent's acknowledgement, genuine contrition, cooperation with OED (providing supplemental responses), lack of prior discipline, and the firm's implementation of procedures to ensure direct communication as factors considered in determining the agreed-upon sanction (public reprimand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and publication options available to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may impose public reprimand and publish the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and in the Official Gazette; disciplinary records may be considered in future matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agreed-Upon Sanction here included a public reprimand, electronic publication at the OED FOIA Reading Room, and an Official Gazette notice materially consistent with the Order. The Order also states the Office may consider the record in future complaints or proceedings as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations by the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional basis for practitioner discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner discipline pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory and regulatory authority under which the Office brings and approves disciplinary matters and settlement agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement/waiver terms in disciplinary resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of a settlement, a practitioner may agree to waive rights to seek reconsideration or review and may agree to bear their own costs; settlements may include waivers of appeal and other procedural rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case, Respondent waived rights to seek reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56, review under § 11.57, and any other appeal or challenge, and each party bore its own costs. Settlement terms may include such procedural waivers and cost allocations.
